extraction.name: POPE
extraction.description: A polling-based query method called POPE (Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation) for better evaluation of object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models, converting the evaluation into a binary classification task.
extraction.creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
extraction.citeAs: Li, Y., Du, Y., Zhou, K., Wang, J., Zhao, W. X., & Wen, J. R. (2023). Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models. arXiv:2305.10355.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The evaluation dataset is constructed by sampling images from the MSCOCO validation set. Ground-truth objects are extracted from human annotations or automatic segmentation tools (SEEM). Negative objects are sampled based on Random, Popular, or Adversarial strategies to form Yes/No questions.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The ratio between ground-truth and nonexistent objects is set as 1:1 for label balance.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For POPE evaluation, 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects in the annotations are randomly selected. For CHAIR evaluation, 2,000 images with annotations about contained objects and human-labeled captions are randomly sampled from the validation set.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Questions whose answers are 'Yes' are built using ground-truth objects, while questions with the answer 'No' are built by sampling from negative objects. Negative objects are sampled under Random (randomly sample objects not in image), Popular (select top-k most frequent objects in dataset not in image), or Adversarial (select top-k frequent objects co-occurring with ground-truth objects not in image) settings.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: When combined with the automatic segmentation tool, the objects would be annotated based on the label set by the tool, which may be inconsistent with the collected human annotations, leading to a divergence in evaluation results.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The hallucination phenomenon hinders the safe use of LVLMs in real-world deployment, as it may result in unexpected consequences caused by these hallucinated objects. For example, due to an incorrect understanding of the external environment, an autonomous driving system would make wrong decisions when encountering unexpected events, which might lead to serious safety issues.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The visual instruction datasets (like MSCOCO) share a similar unbalanced object distribution where top frequent objects occupy a major part of the dataset. LVLMs are prone to hallucinate frequently appearing objects in the visual instruction datasets and objects that frequently co-occur with ground-truth objects in the image.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The evaluation focuses only on object hallucination and cannot measure the overall performance of LVLMs. Evaluation is performed on a part of the validation set, so results might be affected by data distribution. POPE utilizes a matching-based method to determine Yes/No answers, but LVLMs may occasionally fail to provide answers explicitly containing these words. Automatic segmentation tool annotations may be inconsistent with human annotations.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Evaluation of object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models
